description_full: CRH plc, together with its subsidiaries, provides building materials solutions in Ireland, the United States, the United Kingdom, rest of Europe, and internationally. It operates through three segments: Americas Materials Solutions, Americas Building Solutions, and International Solutions. The company offers building materials for the construction and maintenance of public infrastructure, and commercial and residential buildings, as well as construction and renovation of transportation infrastructure, critical utility networks, commercial and residential buildings, and outdoor living spaces; paving and construction services; and produces and sells aggregates, cementitious materials, ready mixed concrete and mortars, and asphalt. It also manufactures, supplies, and delivers building products for the built environment in communities in North America; and provides building and infrastructure solutions for complex critical utility infrastructure, such as water, energy, transportation, and telecommunications projects, and outdoor living solutions for private and public spaces. In addition, the company produces and supplies precast and pre-stressed concrete products comprising vaults, pipes, and manholes; and concrete and polymer-based products, such as underground vaults, drainage systems, enclosures, and modular precast structures for applications in transportation, water, energy, and telecommunications markets. Further, it provides crushed stone, sand, and gravel; granite, limestone, and sandstone; fly ash, pozzolans, synthetic gypsum, calcined clay, and ground granulated blast-furnace slags; fencing and railing systems, lawn and garden products, and packaged concrete mixes; and concrete masonry, hardscape and related products, including pavers, blocks and curbs, retaining walls, and slabs. CRH plc was founded in 1936 and is based in Dublin, Ireland.

financial_summary: CRH PLC is a large-cap basic materials business with a $65.3B market cap on $37.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 9% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 36%.

The business throws off $2.9B in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.50× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.7×.

Shareholder yield of 3.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 50% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Altman Z in the grey zone — financial health warrants monitoring
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 9% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Returns on capital have been remarkably steady for 5 years — durability is the real test of a moat
Insiders are net buyers (80% buy ratio) — insiders sell for many reasons but buy for only one
Large open-market insider purchases (net $1.2M) — management putting its own capital behind the business
36 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Basic Materials sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 5pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.11x).
It accounts for 2.2% of sector revenue and 2.5% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 222 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 28% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 25% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 1.07, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $413.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 53% in the 2020 crash, 39% in the 2022 bear market and 55% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $65.24 (margin of safety -50%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 12%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $25.12 to $150 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: EV/EBITDA 10.7 vs 7.9 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $121 on average, 23% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 9.2% annual cash-flow growth, 6pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 8.6%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.04).
It runs a 36% gross margin and converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.50x.
ROE of 16% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA ($4.1B of cash against $17.7B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.7x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.5% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 77% of profits supports about 9.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.99 and a backlog worth 8% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 7.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 5.6% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 89%.
Insider trading is two-way: 4 purchases and 1 sale over the past year, net $1.2M bought.
It returns 3.4% a year to shareholders (1.8% in buybacks and 1.6% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 36 consecutive years.
people: With about 83,032 employees, each generates about $451K of revenue, 0.7x the Basic Materials median, and revenue has grown 3.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $35K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.6M (12x revenue per employee).
